title: Pacem in Terris (1963)
hookLine: a pope writes on rights and peace, and addresses the letter to all people of good will
tomorrow: Signs of the times (Gaudium et Spes)

lines: TO ALL PEOPLE OF GOOD WILL.
cards: Night, a field outside Bethlehem, and shepherds hear the sky fill with voices. In Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, the song goes: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will."
In Latin, pacem in terris. Those words became the name of a letter from Pope John the Twenty-third. It took the angels' audience too.
It's addressed to bishops, clergy and the faithful, and then, at the end of the greeting, to all men of good will. Anyone could open it and find their name on the envelope.

teach.h: RIGHTS THAT COME WITH BEING HUMAN.
teach.b: First, the list. Pacem in Terris sets out rights that belong to a person simply for being a person: life and what keeps it going, food, clothing, shelter, rest, medical care. The right to learn.
To worship God as conscience directs. To work, to meet with others, to move from place to place, to take part in public life. These aren't favors a government hands out.
They come with being human. Second, the other half, the pairing this block met with Cain. A right in one person brings a duty, in that same person and in everyone around them.

teach.h: EVERY RIGHT HAS A DUTY BESIDE IT.
teach.b: My right to life is my duty to look after it, and your duty to respect it. A society that shouts only about rights, the letter suggests, is building with one hand. Third, what peace stands on.
John the Twenty-third names four things: truth, justice, charity and freedom. Peace here isn't just the quiet after the guns stop. It's a building, and those are its four walls.

Take one away, and the roof sags. A treaty table is a long way from an ordinary week. But truth told at work, a fair deal, care for a neighbor, and room for others to choose are the same four walls, built smaller.

teach.h: ON EARTH PEACE TO MEN OF GOOD WILL.
teach.b: The letter takes good will as something people can practice, one wall at a time.

how: Catholics often pray for peace at Mass in the prayers of the faithful, and Pacem in Terris is still read and taught in Catholic schools, parishes and peace groups as a charter of human rights and duties.

games.q: you're writing a letter about peace. who do you address it to?
o: the Church, and all people of good will.
games.why: John XXIII greeted the bishops, clergy and faithful, and then all men of good will, echoing the angels in Luke 2:14.

practice: Bring to mind one table where people are trying to talk instead of fight: two countries in the news, a city council, a family that has stopped speaking.
Picture them there, tired and wary, still at the table, and give each of the four walls one breath: truth, justice, charity, freedom.
If you pray, hold them before God with the angels' line, on earth peace to men of good will; if you don't, keep that table in mind and wish it well.

wordCard.voice: Pacem in Terris. Peace on earth: rights, duties and four walls, for all people of good will. This week's road: the poor first, work has dignity, one family, our common home, a just wage, from the ground up, and now peace on earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: peace on earth, the letter's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: peace on earth. The angels sang it to anyone of good will. Until tomorrow.
